title: Cline CLI npm Package Compromised via Suspected Cache Poisoning Attack

reading.body:
Cline, an AI coding tool, deployed an automated issue triage system that accepted input from any GitHub user and ran with broad permissions to publish code. A researcher demonstrated that prompt injection could trick this system into executing arbitrary commands, potentially exposing publishing credentials that would give attackers access to distribute software to millions of developers through multiple package repositories.

The system was deployed without adequate human review of AI-generated decisions before they executed. The vulnerability window lasted from December 21, 2025, to February 9, 2026. It would have taken either restricting the AI system's permissions, requiring human approval before credential-sensitive actions, or limiting who could trigger the workflow to prevent this attack surface.

It is not established whether attackers successfully exploited this vulnerability to publish malicious code, though the reporting suggests someone may have attempted to do so during the vulnerability window.

summary:
# Summary

Cline, an open-source AI coding tool used by millions of developers, had a critical security vulnerability between December 21, 2025, and February 9, 2026. The Cline team added an AI-powered issue triage workflow that ran with broad permissions and accepted input from anyone with a GitHub account. Researcher Adnan Khan discovered that attackers could exploit this through prompt injection, tricking the AI into running malicious commands that would install compromised code. This created a pathway to steal publishing credentials that could allow attackers to distribute malware through the VS Code Marketplace, OpenVSX, and NPM to millions of developers worldwide.

Khan attempted to report the vulnerability privately for over a month without receiving a response from Cline's team. After public disclosure on February 9, the vulnerability was fixed within an hour, and Cline rotated all credentials. Evidence suggests someone may have attempted to exploit the weakness by poisoning cached files during the vulnerability window, though no malicious updates were actually published. Cline users should disable auto-updates until the team confirms no unauthorized access occurred.
